reference_title: Soil Stabilization and Modification for Pavements

sections.title: Purpose
sections.summary: Quality control ensures the final product is adequate for its intended use and confirms the contractor performed per plans/specifications (a basis for payment). This chapter identifies the most important control factors for cement, lime, LF/LCF, bituminous, and polymer stabilization.
sections.body: Quality control is essential to ensure the final product will be adequate for its intended use and ensure the contractor has performed in accordance with the plans and specifications, as this is a basis for payment. This chapter identifies those control factors that are most important in soil stabilization construction with cement, lime, lime-fly ash, bituminous additives, and polymer emulsions.
key_points: QC purpose: confirms adequacy for intended use AND contractor compliance with plans/specs (basis for payment)
Chapter organized by stabilizer type: cement (5-2), lime (5-3), LF/LCF (5-4), bituminous/polymer (5-5)
sections.applicability: Frames the QC purpose and organization for the whole chapter.

sections.title: Cement Stabilization QC
sections.summary: Key cement-stabilization QC factors: pulverization (sieve check, 100% passing 1in, >=80% passing No.4), cement content (sieve/spot checks via canvas of known area or tonnage-over-area), moisture content (lab OMC as initial guide, nuclear methods for field checks), uniformity of mixing (visual/trench color check), compaction (sand-cone or nuclear density), and curing (bituminous/polymer/liquid membrane at 0.15-0.30 gal/sq yd).
sections.body: The most important factors from a quality control standpoint in cement stabilization are pulverization, cement content, moisture content, uniformity of mixing, time sequence of operations, compaction, and curing. PULVERIZATION: generally not a problem unless clayey/silty soils are being stabilized; a sieve analysis (No. 4 sieve control) determines percent pulverization -- most specs require 100% passing 1 in (25 mm) and >= 80% passing No. 4 (4.75 mm) at compaction time, exclusive of gravel/stone (<= 2 in / 50 mm maximum size); test at the conclusion of mixing. CEMENT CONTENT: typically expressed as percent dry weight of soil (occasionally by volume, less common due to batching complications); spot checks use a canvas of known area, or an overall check of area covered by a known tonnage. MOISTURE CONTENT: the lab-determined OMC for the soil-additive mixture is the initial field guide, adjusted for in-situ soil moisture at construction start; nuclear methods can check moisture at start and during processing -- field compaction equipment typically imparts more energy than lab equipment, so field OMC may run slightly lower than lab results. UNIFORMITY OF MIXING: visual inspection of trenches dug through the treated depth; uniform color indicates a satisfactory mix, streaking indicates non-uniform mixing; pay special attention to pavement edges. COMPACTION: same equipment as untreated soil of that type; density determined by sand-cone (ASTM D1556) or nuclear (ASTM D6938) methods; check depth of compaction and edge compaction specifically. CURING: a bituminous or polymer emulsion or liquid curing compound is frequently applied over stabilized areas, at 0.15-0.30 gal/sq yd (0.68-1.36 L/sq m); the soil-cement surface must be free of dry/loose material and kept continuously moist until the membrane is applied.
key_points: Pulverization: sieve-based check, typically 100% passing 1in and >=80% passing No.4 at compaction time
Cement content: canvas-of-known-area spot checks, or tonnage-over-area overall check
Moisture content: lab OMC as initial field guide; field OMC often runs slightly lower than lab due to higher field compaction energy
Uniformity of mixing: trench visual inspection -- uniform color = good mix, streaking = non-uniform mix
Compaction: sand-cone (ASTM D1556) or nuclear (ASTM D6938) density testing, with attention to depth and edges
Curing: bituminous/polymer/liquid curing compound at 0.15-0.30 gal/sq yd (0.68-1.36 L/sq m)
sections.applicability: Applies to field quality control of cement-stabilized soil construction.

sections.title: Lime Stabilization QC
sections.summary: Key lime-stabilization QC factors: pulverization/scarification (sieve check, depth control), lime content (canvas spot checks; slurry composition via specific gravity), uniformity of mixing (phenolphthalein indicator turns pink at pH 12.4), compaction (sand-cone/nuclear, max ~1-week delay), and curing (moist or membrane, avoiding carbonation).
sections.body: The most important factors to control during soil-lime construction are pulverization and scarification, lime content, uniformity of mixing, time sequence of operations, compaction, and curing. PULVERIZATION AND SCARIFICATION: a sieve analysis (typically based on material passing the 1 in / 25 mm and No. 4 / 4.75 mm sieves) checks adequacy; depth of scarification/pulverization matters relative to the specified treatment depth; for heavy clays, pretreatment with lime aids pulverization, though this may leave agglomerated soil-lime fractions that are easily broken by kneading (not necessarily improper pulverization). LIME CONTENT: application rate can be checked with a canvas of known area, weighing the spread lime; for slurry, the quantity needed for the desired lime solids requires knowing slurry composition, checked via hydrometer or volumetric-weight procedure. UNIFORMITY OF MIXING: the major and most difficult QC goal, since lime-mixed soil looks similar to untreated soil; phenolphthalein indicator solution is recommended -- the soil turns reddish pink when free lime is present (pH = 12.4), indicating minimum lime content; alternatively, collect soil samples at various locations/depths for field-portable pH testing. COMPACTION: proper moisture/density control is most important, using sand-cone (ASTM D1556) or nuclear (ASTM D6938) density and oven-dry (ASTM D2216) or nuclear moisture methods; time between mixing and compacting has a pronounced effect on properties -- begin compaction ASAP, with the National Lime Association recommending an absolute maximum delay of one week; phenolphthalein indicator also helps target density-testing locations by distinguishing properly treated areas from lightly wind-dusted areas. CURING: essential for final properties; either moist curing (light sprinkling + light rolling) or membrane curing (bituminous seal coat or liquid curing compound); regardless of method, protect the entire compacted layer to prevent lime carbonation (inadequate sprinkling that lets the surface dry promotes carbonation).
key_points: Pulverization/scarification: sieve check (1in and No.4 typical); heavy-clay agglomerations from lime pretreatment are not necessarily a defect
Lime content: canvas spot checks for spread rate; slurry composition checked via hydrometer or volumetric-weight
Uniformity of mixing: phenolphthalein indicator solution turns reddish pink at pH 12.4, confirming free-lime presence
Compaction: sand-cone/nuclear density; begin ASAP after mixing, National Lime Association max delay ~1 week
Curing: moist curing or membrane curing; protect against carbonation (surface drying deactivates lime)
sections.applicability: Applies to field quality control of lime-stabilized soil construction.

sections.title: Lime-Fly Ash (LF) and Lime-Cement-Fly Ash (LCF) QC
sections.summary: The nature of LF and LCF stabilization is similar to lime-only stabilization, so the same quality control factors (pulverization, content, uniformity of mixing, compaction, curing) are suggested.
sections.body: The nature of LF and LCF stabilization is similar to that for lime only. Consequently, the same factors involved for quality control are suggested.
key_points: LF/LCF QC largely mirrors the lime-stabilization QC factors of Sec 5-3 (pulverization, content, uniformity of mixing, compaction, curing)
sections.applicability: Applies to field quality control of LF and LCF stabilized-soil construction; defers to Sec 5-3 lime QC procedures.

sections.title: Bituminous and Polymer Stabilization QC
sections.summary: Key bituminous/polymer QC factors: moisture content (below optimum for polymer), asphalt viscosity/temperature (>=50F), asphalt/polymer content (spot checks, percent solids for polymer), uniformity of mixing (color-change check for emulsions), aeration ('tacky/crawling' criterion), compaction (roll when emulsion 'breaks'), and curing (2-5 day recommendation for emulsified bases).
sections.body: The factors that seem most important to control during construction with bituminous and polymer stabilization are moisture content, viscosity of the liquid, additive content, uniformity of mixing, aeration, compaction, and curing. MOISTURE CONTENT: determined by oven-drying (ASTM D2216) or nuclear methods (ASTM D6938); the Asphalt Institute recommends up to 3%+ surface moisture for emulsified asphalt and < 3% for cutback asphalt; higher-PI soils need higher moisture; for polymer emulsions, keep starting soil moisture well below optimum (the emulsion's own water otherwise pushes it above optimum, lowering compacted density) -- asphalt emulsion tolerates this better due to its lubricating coating. VISCOSITY OF ASPHALT: avoid cold-mix construction below 50 degF (10 degC), since asphalt rapidly reaches aggregate temperature and mixing becomes difficult; cutback asphalts occasionally need heating; emulsions need to stay above their minimum film-forming temperature. ASPHALT AND POLYMER CONTENT: maintain at or slightly below optimum for the specified mix (excess asphalt causes compaction difficulty and hot-weather plastic deformation); polymer content is computed from percent solids of the emulsion, checked at random for delivered-product consistency. UNIFORMITY OF MIXING: visual inspection; emulsified asphalts show a brown-to-black color change when broken; the Asphalt Institute recommends controlling travel speed, aggregate volume, and emulsion flow rate for mixed-in-place uniformity (an above-design asphalt content is sometimes needed to assure uniform mixing); polymer-stabilized soil uniformity is less visually obvious, requiring extra care to confirm full-depth mixing. AERATION: allow diluents to evaporate before compaction (an unaerated mix cannot be compacted to acceptable limits); the mixture has aerated when it becomes tacky and 'crawls'; overmixing in central-plant mixes can cause emulsions to break early, making the mix difficult to work. COMPACTION: begin once aeration is complete; rolling should begin as an emulsified mixture starts to break (brown-to-black); early compaction causes undue rutting/shoving; emulsion-stabilized bases often reach higher density than unstabilized bases for the same compaction effort. CURING: the greatest QC challenge in asphalt soil stabilization -- rate depends on asphalt quantity, humidity, wind, rain, sunlight, and temperature; initial curing (diluent evaporation) occurs during aeration and must support compaction equipment; starting compaction too early seals the pavement, delaying dehydration and design-strength attainment; the Asphalt Institute recommends a 2-5 day curing period for emulsified bases under favorable conditions; cement can accelerate curing; polymeric emulsions cure by water evaporation, so a curing membrane is not recommended for them.
key_points: Moisture: below-optimum starting soil moisture is essential for polymer emulsions (unlike asphalt emulsion, which tolerates it better)
Viscosity/temperature: avoid cold-mix construction below 50F (10C)
Content: maintain at or slightly below optimum; excess causes compaction problems and hot-weather deformation
Uniformity: emulsion color change (brown-to-black) signals mixing progress; polymer uniformity needs extra visual care (less obvious)
Aeration: mix is ready when 'tacky and crawls'; overmixing can cause premature emulsion breaking
Compaction: begin as emulsion 'breaks' (color change); early compaction causes rutting/shoving
Curing: 2-5 day recommendation for emulsified bases (Asphalt Institute); polymeric emulsions should NOT get a curing membrane (they cure by water evaporation)
sections.applicability: Applies to field quality control of bituminous- and polymer-emulsion stabilized-soil construction.
